title: UNIT 3: ELASTICITY AND STATIC EQUILIBRIUM OF RIGID BODY
notes:
✓ Force → Can change the shape or size of a body.

✓ Some materials → Regain their original shape after the deforming force is removed, while others remain permanently deformed.

title: 3.1 ELASTICITY AND PLASTICITY
notes:
◆ RIGID BODY
✓ Rigid body → An idealized hard solid having a definite shape and size. In reality, every solid can be deformed when a sufficiently large external force is applied.

◆ DEFORMING FORCE
✓ Deforming force → A force that changes the shape or size of a body.

◆ ELASTICITY
✓ Elasticity → Property of a body by which it regains its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.

✓ Elastic deformation → Temporary deformation that disappears when the force is removed.

◆ Examples
Rubber • metals • steel ropes • springs.

◆ PLASTICITY
✓ Plasticity → Property of a body by which it does not regain its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.

✓ Plastic deformation → Permanent and irreversible change in shape or size caused by a sustained deforming force.

◆ Examples
Putty • potter's clay • permanently bent materials.

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Elastic → Returns to original shape.
✓ Plastic → Remains permanently deformed.

◆ ELASTIC LIMIT
✓ Elastic limit → The limit up to which a material remains elastic. Beyond the elastic limit, permanent deformation occurs.

title: 3.2 DENSITY AND SPECIFIC GRAVITY
notes:
◆ DENSITY
✓ Density → Mass contained in a unit volume of a substance.

ρ = m/V

✓ ρ → Density.
✓ m → Mass.
✓ V → Volume.
✓ SI unit → kg/m³.
✓ Another common unit → g/cm³.

✓ 1 kg/m³ = 10⁻³ g/cm³.

◆ FACTORS AFFECTING DENSITY
Temperature
Pressure
Arrangement of atoms
Nature of the substance

◆ FLOATING & SINKING
✓ Object density > surrounding fluid density → Object generally sinks.
✓ Object density < surrounding fluid density → Object generally floats.

✓ Example → Oil is less dense than water, so it floats on water.

◆ SPECIFIC GRAVITY
✓ Specific gravity (SG) → Ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a standard substance.

✓ For liquids and solids → Water at 4°C is commonly used as the reference because water has its maximum density at 4°C.

SG = ρsubstance/ρwater

✓ Specific gravity → Has no unit because it is a ratio of two densities.

◆ APPLICATIONS
Determining mineral content of rocks.
Comparing the purity of gemstones.
Comparing the densities of substances.

title: 3.3 STRESS AND STRAIN
notes:
✓ Deformation → Can occur through squashing, squeezing, twisting, shearing or pulling.

✓ Stress and strain → Describe the forces producing deformation and the resulting deformation.

◆ STRESS
✓ Stress → Deforming force acting per unit area.

Stress = F/A

✓ SI unit → N/m² = Pa.

◆ TYPES OF STRESS
✓ Tensile stress → Pulls a body apart and tends to elongate it.
✓ Compressive stress → Pushes/squeezes a body and tends to shorten it.
✓ Bulk/volume stress → Squeezes a body from all sides and changes its volume.
✓ Shear stress → Tangential forces deform the shape of a body.

◆ STRAIN
✓ Strain → Fractional measure of deformation produced by stress. It is dimensionless.

◆ TYPES OF STRAIN
✓ Tensile/linear strain:
ε = ΔL/L₀

✓ ΔL → Change in length.
✓ L₀ → Original length.

✓ Volumetric strain:
εᵥ = ΔV/V₀

✓ ΔV → Change in volume.
✓ V₀ → Original volume.

✓ Shearing strain:
Shear strain = Δx/L₀

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Stress → Cause of deformation.
✓ Strain → Measure of the resulting deformation.

title: 3.3 HOOKE'S LAW & ELASTIC MODULUS
notes:
◆ HOOKE'S LAW
✓ Within the elastic limit → Stress is directly proportional to the corresponding strain.

Stress ∝ Strain

Stress = k × Strain

✓ k → Modulus of elasticity.

◆ ELASTIC MODULUS
✓ Modulus of elasticity → Measures how strongly a material resists deformation.

✓ Large elastic modulus → Smaller deformation for a given stress.
✓ Small elastic modulus → Larger deformation for the same stress.

◆ THREE ELASTIC MODULI
✓ Young modulus → Tensile/compressive deformation.
✓ Bulk modulus → Volume deformation.
✓ Shear modulus → Shape deformation due to shear stress.

title: 3.4 THE YOUNG MODULUS
notes:
✓ Young modulus → Elastic modulus associated with tensile or compressive deformation.

◆ DEFINITION
✓ Young modulus = Tensile stress / Tensile strain

Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L₀)

✓ Therefore:
Y = FL₀/(AΔL)

✓ F → Deforming force.
✓ A → Cross-sectional area.
✓ L₀ → Original length.
✓ ΔL → Change in length.

◆ UNIT
✓ SI unit → N/m² or Pa.

◆ PHYSICAL MEANING
✓ Young modulus → Measures the resistance of a material to a change in its length.

✓ Large Y → Material is harder to stretch/compress.
✓ Small Y → Material deforms more easily.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ For a material in its elastic range → The relationship between tensile stress and tensile strain is linear.

◆ LIMITATION
✓ Young modulus → Is meaningful for deformation within the elastic range.

✓ Permanent deformation occurs → The simple elastic relationship no longer applies.

title: 3.5 STATIC EQUILIBRIUM
notes:
✓ Static equilibrium → Occurs when an object or system remains at rest and does not tilt or rotate. All forces and torques acting on it are balanced.

◆ CONDITIONS FOR EQUILIBRIUM
✓ Rigid body in equilibrium →
Net external force = 0.
Net external torque = 0.

✓ These → Are called the first and second conditions of equilibrium.

◆ FREE-BODY DIAGRAM
✓ Free-body diagram → Shows all external forces acting on an object and is useful for checking the conditions of equilibrium.

◆ EXAMPLES
Book resting on a table.
Beam supported by a structure.
Balanced seesaw.
Object suspended by cables.

title: 3.5.1 FIRST CONDITION OF EQUILIBRIUM
notes:
✓ First condition → Requires the vector sum of all external forces acting on the body to be zero.

ΣF = 0

✓ For one-dimensional forces:
ΣFx = 0

✓ For two-dimensional forces:
ΣFx = 0
ΣFy = 0

✓ First condition → Means there is no translational acceleration.

◆ IMPORTANT
✓ Static equilibrium → Object at rest.
✓ Dynamic equilibrium → Object moves with constant velocity.

✓ Zero net force → Does not necessarily mean zero velocity; it means zero acceleration.

title: 3.5.2 SECOND CONDITION OF EQUILIBRIUM
notes:
✓ Second condition → Requires the net external torque acting on the body to be zero.

Στ = 0

◆ TORQUE
✓ Torque → Twisting effect of a force about an axis or pivot.

τ = Fr sin θ

✓ F → Force.
✓ r → Distance from the pivot.
✓ θ → Angle between the force and the position vector.

✓ If the force is perpendicular to the lever arm:
τ = Fr

◆ TORQUE DEPENDS ON
✓ Magnitude of force.
✓ Distance from the pivot.
✓ Angle at which the force acts.

◆ CLOCKWISE & COUNTERCLOCKWISE TORQUE
✓ Rotational equilibrium → Total clockwise torque = total counterclockwise torque.

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ ΣF = 0 → No translational acceleration.
✓ Στ = 0 → No rotational acceleration.

✓ Static equilibrium → Requires both conditions to be satisfied for a rigid body to remain in equilibrium.

title: 3.5 STATIC EQUILIBRIUM APPLICATIONS
notes:
✓ Static equilibrium principles → Are used in everyday structures and objects.

◆ BOOK ON TABLE
✓ Downward weight → Is balanced by the upward supporting force.

◆ SEESAW
✓ Seesaw → Is balanced when the clockwise and counterclockwise torques about the pivot are equal.

◆ BEAMS & SUPPORTS
✓ Supported beam → Remains stationary when:
ΣF = 0

and

Στ = 0

◆ DOOR
✓ Force applied farther from the hinge → Produces greater torque than the same force applied closer to the hinge.

✓ Key idea → Increasing the distance from the pivot increases the turning effect for the same perpendicular force.

title: UNIT 3: QUICK REVISION
notes:
◆ ELASTICITY
✓ Ability to regain original shape and size after deforming force is removed.

◆ PLASTICITY
✓ Permanent deformation after the force is removed.

◆ DEFORMING FORCE
✓ Force that changes shape or size.

◆ DENSITY
✓ ρ = m/V.

◆ SPECIFIC GRAVITY
✓ SG = ρsubstance/ρwater; unitless.

◆ STRESS
✓ Stress = F/A; unit = Pa.

◆ TENSILE
✓ Stretching.

◆ COMPRESSIVE
✓ Squeezing/shortening.

◆ BULK
✓ Compression from all sides; volume changes.

◆ SHEAR
✓ Tangential deformation; shape changes.

◆ TENSILE STRAIN
✓ ΔL/L₀.

◆ VOLUMETRIC STRAIN
✓ ΔV/V₀.

◆ SHEAR STRAIN
✓ Δx/L₀.

◆ HOOKE'S LAW
✓ Within elastic limit → Stress ∝ Strain.

◆ YOUNG MODULUS
✓ Y = Tensile stress/Tensile strain = FL₀/(AΔL).

◆ STATIC EQUILIBRIUM
✓ Body at rest with balanced forces and torques.

◆ FIRST CONDITION
✓ ΣF = 0.

◆ SECOND CONDITION
✓ Στ = 0.

◆ TORQUE
✓ τ = Fr sin θ; for perpendicular force, τ = Fr.

✓ MASTER IDEA → Elasticity describes deformation and recovery; stress and strain quantify deformation; Young modulus measures resistance to length change; equilibrium requires both translational and rotational balance.
